items.stem: By the mid-1930s the League of Nations had lost much of its authority. (a) Describe how the failures of the League in the 1930s affected international relations. [4] (b) Why did the failure of the League make war more likely? [6]
items.answer: (a) Japan kept Manchuria and left the League in 1933. Italy conquered Abyssinia and left the League in 1937. Collective security was discredited. Dictators believed they could use force without being stopped. Countries such as Britain and France turned to appeasement and rearmament instead. (b) Aggressors learned that the League would not stop them. Collective security was replaced by every country looking after itself. Britain and France turned to appeasement. Italy and Japan moved closer to Germany, forming the Axis.

items.stem: In 1919 many Germans swore that they would overturn the Treaty of Versailles. ‘The Treaty of Versailles was the main reason for the outbreak of war in 1939.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Resentment of the treaty helped Hitler win power and support for his foreign policy. German minorities in Czechoslovakia and Poland gave Hitler his targets. Against: The failure of the League allowed aggression to go unpunished. The Depression helped Hitler to power and made Britain and France reluctant to act. Hitler's own aims, such as Lebensraum, went far beyond overturning the treaty. Appeasement and the Nazi-Soviet Pact made war possible in 1939. Judgement: The treaty created grievances, but war came in 1939 because Hitler set out to go beyond them and other powers failed to stop him in time.

items.stem: In 1919 many Germans swore that they would overturn the Treaty of Versailles. (a) Describe the German grievances about the Treaty of Versailles that Hitler exploited. [4] (b) Why did the Treaty of Versailles help to cause the Second World War? [6]
items.answer: (a) War guilt was seen as a lie and a humiliation. Reparations were blamed for economic hardship. Military restrictions left Germany weaker than its neighbours. Germans were placed under foreign rule, for example in the Polish Corridor and the Sudetenland. Union with Austria was forbidden. (b) It created resentment that Hitler exploited to win support. It left Germany weakened but not destroyed, so it could recover and seek revenge. It left German minorities in Czechoslovakia and Poland, which gave Hitler excuses for expansion. It was not enforced: Britain came to feel it was too harsh and allowed Hitler to break it.

items.stem: When Hitler came to power in 1933, he promised to overturn the Treaty of Versailles. (a) What were Hitler's foreign policy aims? [4] (b) Why was the Anschluss important? [6]

items.stem: Between 1933 and 1938 Hitler broke several terms of the Treaty of Versailles. Describe how Hitler achieved the Anschluss in 1938.
items.answer: Hitler pressured the Austrian Chancellor Schuschnigg to give Nazis posts in government. Schuschnigg called a plebiscite on Austrian independence. Hitler forced him to cancel it and resign. German troops entered Austria on 12 March 1938. A plebiscite controlled by the Nazis recorded over 99 per cent in favour of union.

items.stem: When Hitler came to power in 1933, he promised to overturn the Treaty of Versailles. ‘Hitler had a clear plan for war from the start.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Mein Kampf set out aims of overturning Versailles and gaining Lebensraum in the east. The Hossbach Memorandum of 1937 recorded Hitler discussing expansion by force. He rearmed rapidly from 1933. Against: Hitler often took advantage of opportunities, as with the Rhineland during the Abyssinian crisis. He was cautious and gambled, ready to retreat in the Rhineland. The Anschluss was hurried when Schuschnigg called a plebiscite. Others' weakness (appeasement) shaped his timing. Judgement: Hitler had clear long-term aims, but he was an opportunist about the timing and methods; the outcome also depended on how others responded.

items.stem: In September 1938 Chamberlain flew to Germany three times to meet Hitler. Describe the events of the Sudeten crisis in September 1938.
items.answer: Hitler demanded the Sudetenland, claiming Sudeten Germans were mistreated. Chamberlain met Hitler at Berchtesgaden on 15 September and agreed to parts of the Sudetenland being handed over. At Bad Godesberg on 22 September Hitler demanded all of it by 1 October. Europe prepared for war and Britain dug trenches and issued gas masks. At Munich on 29-30 September Britain, France and Italy agreed Germany could take the Sudetenland.

items.stem: What were the terms of the Munich Agreement?
items.answer: Germany would occupy the Sudetenland in stages from 1 October 1938. An international commission would decide other disputed areas. Czechoslovakia was not consulted. Britain and France promised to guarantee what was left of Czechoslovakia. Hitler and Chamberlain also signed a separate declaration that Britain and Germany would never go to war again.

items.stem: In September 1938 Chamberlain flew to Germany three times to meet Hitler. ‘Chamberlain was right to follow a policy of appeasement.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Britain was not ready for war in 1938 and used the year to build fighters and radar. Public opinion and the Dominions did not support war over the Sudetenland. Many believed German grievances over Versailles were genuine. It showed that Britain had tried everything, uniting the country when war came in 1939. Against: It encouraged Hitler to make further demands. Czechoslovakia's army and defences were abandoned. Germany also used the time to rearm. It made Stalin distrust the West, leading to the Nazi-Soviet Pact. Judgement: Appeasement was understandable given Britain's position and public opinion, but it misjudged Hitler and made war more likely on worse terms.

items.stem: How far was appeasement responsible for the outbreak of war in 1939? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It allowed Hitler to grow stronger with each success. It convinced Hitler that Britain and France would not fight for Poland. It pushed Stalin towards the Nazi-Soviet Pact. Against: Hitler's aims of Lebensraum made war likely anyway. The Nazi-Soviet Pact removed the danger of a two-front war. The failure of the League and the Depression had already weakened the peace. Judgement: Appeasement did not cause the war, but it made it more likely by encouraging Hitler and failing to build an alliance with the USSR.

He needed time to build up the Red Army, weakened by the purges. The pact gave him land in Poland and the Baltic states as a buffer zone.

items.stem: ‘The Nazi-Soviet Pact was the most important reason for the outbreak of war in 1939.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It removed the danger of a two-front war, allowing Hitler to invade Poland. It divided Poland between Germany and the USSR, making the invasion safe. Against: Hitler's aim of Lebensraum meant war in the east was always likely. Appeasement had convinced Hitler that Britain and France would not fight. The failures of the League and the Treaty of Versailles created the conditions for war. Judgement: The pact was the immediate trigger that made war in September 1939 possible, but the deeper causes lay in Hitler's aims and the earlier failure to stop him.

The USSR would have a sphere of influence over the Baltic states and Bessarabia. A separate trade agreement gave Germany Soviet raw materials.

items.stem: ‘The Treaty of Versailles was the main reason for the outbreak of war in 1939.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Resentment of the treaty helped Hitler win power and support for his foreign policy. German minorities in Czechoslovakia and Poland gave Hitler his targets. Against: The failure of the League allowed aggression to go unpunished. The Depression helped Hitler to power and made Britain and France reluctant to act. Hitler's own aims, such as Lebensraum, went far beyond overturning the treaty. Appeasement and the Nazi-Soviet Pact made war possible in 1939. Judgement: The treaty created grievances, but war came in 1939 because Hitler set out to go beyond them and other powers failed to stop him in time.

items.stem: What is meant by “Anschluss”?

The union of Germany and Austria, carried out by Hitler in March 1938.
The 1936 agreement between Germany and Japan against communism, joined by Italy in 1937.
The border region of Czechoslovakia with about three million German-speaking people.
items.answer: The union of Germany and Austria, carried out by Hitler in March 1938.

items.stem: When Hitler came to power in 1933, he promised to overturn the Treaty of Versailles. What were Hitler's foreign policy aims?
items.answer: To overturn the Treaty of Versailles. To rearm Germany. To unite all German-speaking people in a Greater Germany. To gain Lebensraum (living space) in eastern Europe. To destroy communism and the USSR.

items.stem: How important was the remilitarisation of the Rhineland as a turning point in Hitler's foreign policy? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It was his first use of troops to break Versailles and Locarno. Its success showed Britain and France would not act and increased his confidence. Fortifications in the west made it harder for France to help its eastern allies. Against: Rearmament from 1933-35 had already broken the treaty. The Anschluss and Munich added more territory and resources. The Nazi-Soviet Pact was the decisive step towards war. Judgement: The Rhineland was a crucial gamble that changed the balance of power, but the Anschluss and Munich did more to make further expansion possible.

items.stem: Between 1933 and 1938 Hitler broke several terms of the Treaty of Versailles. (a) Why did Britain and France not stop the remilitarisation of the Rhineland? [6] (b) ‘Hitler had a clear plan for war from the start.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [10]
items.answer: (a) France was in the middle of an election campaign and would not act without Britain. Many in Britain thought Germany was only moving into its own territory. Both were distracted by the Abyssinian crisis. They overestimated German strength and feared war. (b) For: Mein Kampf set out aims of overturning Versailles and gaining Lebensraum in the east. The Hossbach Memorandum of 1937 recorded Hitler discussing expansion by force. He rearmed rapidly from 1933. Against: Hitler often took advantage of opportunities, as with the Rhineland during the Abyssinian crisis. He was cautious and gambled, ready to retreat in the Rhineland. The Anschluss was hurried when Schuschnigg called a plebiscite. Others' weakness (appeasement) shaped his timing. Judgement: Hitler had clear long-term aims, but he was an opportunist about the timing and methods; the outcome also depended on how others responded.

items.stem: At Munich in September 1938 Britain and France agreed that Germany could take the Sudetenland. What were the terms of the Munich Agreement?
items.answer: Germany would occupy the Sudetenland in stages from 1 October 1938. An international commission would decide other disputed areas. Czechoslovakia was not consulted. Britain and France promised to guarantee what was left of Czechoslovakia. Hitler and Chamberlain also signed a separate declaration that Britain and Germany would never go to war again.

items.stem: How important was the failure of the League of Nations in causing the Second World War? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Manchuria and Abyssinia showed collective security had failed. Hitler learned that aggression would not be punished. Against: Hitler's aims would probably have led to war anyway. Appeasement by Britain and France was a separate policy choice. The Nazi-Soviet Pact removed the threat of a two-front war. Judgement: The League's failure was important because it removed the main obstacle to aggression, but it did not itself cause war; Hitler's policies did.

items.stem: Describe the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in 1936.
items.answer: German troops marched into the Rhineland on 7 March 1936. This broke the Treaty of Versailles and the Locarno Treaties. Hitler gave orders to retreat if the French resisted. The world was distracted by the Abyssinian crisis. Britain and France protested but did not act; many British people thought Germany was "walking into its own back garden".
